title: Designing a 4-5 m Wide Tube House: Smart Space Planning
desc: How to plan a tube house with a 4-5 m frontage: front-middle-rear zoning, stairs, bathrooms, light well, parking, and rules on density and projections.
summary: Space-planning principles for a narrow 4-5 m frontage tube house: zoning, placing stairs, bathrooms and light well, parking, and the rules to check before designing.
body: p

The tube house (nhà ống, a narrow townhouse) with a 4-5 m frontage and 15-25 m depth is the most common house type in cities. A narrow, long plot often leaves the middle rooms dark and stuffy, stairs take up space, and motorbikes encroach on the living room. This article summarises the planning principles architects commonly apply to make the house bright, airy and easy to use.
h2
1. Divide the house into three zones: front, middle, rear
p
A simple and effective approach is to divide the plan along its depth:
ul
Front zone (facing the street): parking, living room or business space. This is the noisiest and dustiest zone, so put the shared living functions here.
Middle zone: stairs, bathrooms, light well or void. Gathering the “technical” parts in the middle gives both ends of the house regular-shaped rooms that receive light.
Rear zone: kitchen and dining on the ground floor; bedrooms on the upper floors. If possible, leave a small rear yard for air and drying clothes.
p

For a house deeper than 18-20 m, a light well in the middle is almost essential if the middle rooms are to have natural light. See also how to build a light well properly in the article on natural ventilation.
h2
2. Stairs: their position decides the whole plan
ul
In the middle of the house, beside the light well: short travel, divides the house into two balanced parts, and light from the well reaches the stairs too.
Against one side wall: leaves the rest open and continuous, suited to a 4 m frontage.
Avoid putting the stairs right next to the main door if the ground floor is used for business or parking - it is both obstructive and reduces privacy for the upper floors.
h2
3. Bathrooms, kitchen and pipes
p

Stack the bathrooms on each floor directly above one another and near a shared service duct. Short supply and drainage pipes with few bends are less likely to block, are easier to repair and reduce the risk of leaks into the room below. Put the kitchen at the rear, near the rear yard or light well to let odours escape; avoid a kitchen in the middle of the house without a window or an extractor vented outside.
p
Rainwater and wastewater must be led to the common drainage system and not discharged onto the neighbouring house; this is the owner's obligation under Article 250 and Article 251 of the Civil Code.
h2
4. Parking and the facade
ul
A 4 m frontage can hold about 2-3 motorbikes plus a walkway; to park a car you need to calculate carefully the door width, the ground-floor beam height and the access from the pavement.
The main door should be wide, with a side door or vent panel to let air in when closed.

Balconies, canopies and entrance roofs that project must follow the detailed plan, urban design and architectural management regulations of the area; they must not go past the red line where the house has a setback, and must not cross the plot boundary into the neighbouring house (Sections 2.5.7 and 2.5.8 of QCVN 01:2026/BXD, applicable from 1 January 2027).
h2
5. Rules to check before drawing
ul

Building density: under Table 8 of QCVN 01:2026/BXD, a single-family house plot up to 90 m² may be built to a maximum of 100%, a 100 m² plot 90%, and a 200 m² plot 70% (Section 2.5.3). The area's detailed plan may set stricter limits.

Who may design: for a house under 3 floors, without a basement, with total floor area under 250 m² and under 12 m high, the owner may organise the design personally; a larger house must be designed by an organisation or individual with the relevant expertise (Clause 2, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP). See also Designing your own house: when you must hire a design firm.
Building permit: most townhouses must apply for one; see Procedure for a building permit for a single-family house.
h2
6. Small tips for narrow houses
ul
Use glass partitions and sliding doors instead of built walls between shared spaces so light reaches deeper.
Avoid exposed beams and overly low dropped ceilings on the ground floor - a narrow house needs a sense of height and openness.
Built-in cabinets, and the space under the stairs used for storage or a secondary toilet, make use of the area.
The top floor should have a terrace or a sunshade roof to reduce heat for the whole house.
p

Every plot differs in orientation, depth, access alley and family needs. If you are preparing to build a townhouse, Quan Construction can advise on layout options and prepare the design dossier - contact us.
note

This article is for reference; every work needs to be surveyed and designed by a qualified person. QCVN 01:2026/BXD takes effect on 1 January 2027; the specific indicators for each plot follow the detailed plan, urban design and architectural management regulations where you build.
